content.abstract:
Twenty Fifth Indian Antarctic Expedition 2006-2007
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 23, pp 73-105
Climatic History and Landscape Evolution of 
Schirmacher Oasis, East Antarctica during Late 
Quaternary: A multi-proxy study
Binita Phartiyal
Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeobotany, 53-University Road, 
Lucknow-226007, U.P., India
ABSTRACT
Schirmacher Oasis (SO) region of East Antarctica is known for 118 lakes, 
broadly categorized into pro-glacial, land locked and epi-shelf lakes. During the 
XXV ISEA 2005-06, mapping of the palaeolakes and the dry lake beds of the 
region of East Antarctica was done. Based on distribution of the sediment cover 
and detailed lithological, sedimentological and chronological study of ten profiles 
in -35 sq km of the SO region, five areas have been mapped that were occupied by 
large lakes during the Holocene. The water bodies were present from the Holocene 
(-10,000 to 3000 years BP) and have reduced in size by negative water balance. 
This desiccation can possibly be attributed to the combined effect of recession of 
glaciers feeding them, low melt water, low precipitation and strong winds. Several 
of these lakes have been reduced in size to mere lake-lets and ponds. These lacustrine 
sediment fills are a very important source of information to trace the Quatemaiy 
geological history and palaeoclimatic records from the southern Hemisphere. From 
the detailed lithology of sediment profiles a landform reconstruction from 13,000 
years BP to the present is also proposed. Apart from this a high resolution mineral 
magnetic investigation has been carried out in few of these sections which have a 
defined chronology to reconstruct past climatic condition. The parameters included 
concentration dependent (%, ARM and SIRM), independent (S-ratio, ARM/SIRM) 
and some interprametric ratios (%fd %, SIRM/%, SIRM/ARM, S-Ratio, hard and 
soft IRM’s) wfi^li were used to document regional palaeoclimatic changes in the 
eastern part of Antarctica. Magnetite is the primary of remenance in these sediments 
and fall in SP and SD grain size range. The LOI% indicates a very low organic 
content. Elements in order of abundance present in these sediments are Fe, Rb, Zn, 
Mo, Co, Pb, Mn, Cu and As, with Fe being the most abundant followed by Rb and 
others present in minor amounts. The mineral magnetic data supplemented with 
the radiocarbon chronology (AMS) traces 6 phases of climatic fluctuation between 
13-3 ka BP from this region (Phase 1, 3 and 5 representing cold glacial periods 
while Phases 2,4, and 6 being warmer periods). There was one short warm period 
~ 12.5 ka BP (Phase 2) and two marked warm periods within the Holocene, one

74 Binita Phartiyal
between 11.5-9 ka BP (Phase 4), and one between 4-3 ka BP (Phase 6). The 
maximum susceptibility and the other ratios correspond to the glacial period and 
minimum reflect the interglacial, lacustrine phase i.e., a comparatively warmer 
phase. Holocene Optima (Phase 4) and Mid Holocene Hypsithermal (MHH) (Phase 6) 
are distinctively seen with a decrease in the value concentration dependent 
parameters.
INTRODUCTION
The lakes in ice-free regions of Antarctica are unique on this planet. 
The persistent ice covers them for 6-8 months a year, minimizes wind­
generated currents and reduces light penetration, as well as restricts sediment 
deposition into the lake. These are modem-day equivalents of periglacial 
lakes that were common during glacial periods at temperate latitudes and 
offer an important record of catchment and environmental changes.
Only 0.8% of Antarctica is ice free while 99.2% is covered by ice, 
therefore this continent has not been as well documented for climatic data 
during the Late Quaternary as the Northern Hemisphere, with defined Bond 
cycles, Heinrich events, Last Glacial Maxima, Younger Dryas and Older 
Dryas, Holocene optima, DO cycles etc. (Johnsen et al. 1992, Bond et al.
1992, 1993, 1995, Dansgaard et al. 1993, Heinrich 1998, Broecker 2002 
and many more). Although only a minor part of this southern continent is 
ice free (Fig. 1), it still offers a great prospective for such kind of studies 
from the southern hemisphere too. There are a number of ice-free areas in 
the eastern coast of Antarctica-the Bunger hills in the Wright valley, 
McMurdo valley in Southern Victoria land the Schirmacher Oasis in Queen 
Maud land, are some of them and have been studied by many researchers 
for various disciplines since the 1950’s. (Korotkevich 1958, Wilson and 
Wellman 1962, Hoare 1966, Gumbley et al. 1974, Wilson 1979, Matsubaya 
et al. 1979, Lyons et al. 1985, 1998; Kaup et al. 1993, Smith and Friedman
1993, Doran et al. 2004 and many more). SO region in east Antarctica is 
just a little speck of 35 sq km area on the eastern part of 14 million sq km 
area of Antarctica (Fig. 1) and is a treasure trove for Quaternary researchers 
as most part of the SO is sediment fill of lakes in the geological past
